specPoints.text: understand factors that influence the choice of solvents, including: i water, to dissolve some ionic compounds, in terms of the hydration of the ions ii water, to dissolve simple alcohols, in terms of hydrogen bonding iii water, as a poor solvent for compounds (to include polar molecules such as halogenoalkane), in terms of inability to form hydrogen bonds iv non-aqueous solvents, for compounds that have similar intermolecular forces to those in the solvent Further suggested practicals: i the solubility of simple molecules in different solvents ii measuring the enthalpy change of vaporisation of water iii measuring temperature changes when substances dissolve

primer.text: Dissolving is a contest of attractions: solute particles against solvent particles, with the winner decided by matching force types. This note explains why water hydrates ions yet rejects haloalkanes, why long alcohol chains fade from view, and why giant covalent lattices resist every solvent you can pour on them.

lessons.title: Like dissolves like
lessons.opening: Solvents pick partners whose forces match their own. This lesson states the like-dissolves-like principle, follows ethanol's hydrogen bonds into water, watches hexanol fade from view as its chain grows, and counts what a giant covalent lattice demands of any solvent.
keyPoints: Non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents through dispersion forces on both sides.
Polar covalent solutes dissolve in polar solvents through dipole-dipole interactions or hydrogen bonds.
Ethanol mixes with water because hydrogen bonds form between the two molecules.
Solubility fades as the non-polar chain grows: ethanol dissolves readily, hexanol barely.
Giant covalent lattices dissolve in nothing, because breaking their covalent network costs too much energy.

low.restatement: Matching force types lets solute and solvent swap partners smoothly; mismatched forces leave the solute stranded, and size eventually outvotes any single polar group.
low.analogy: A guest joins a dinner party only if they speak the same language (matching forces); one fluent guest in a huge silent hall (long chain) barely changes the conversation.
low.examPointer: Quote ethanol versus hexanol by formula - C2H5OH dissolves readily while C6H13OH does not - when the question asks for evidence of the chain-length effect.

medium.restatement: Dissolution competes: solute-solute and solvent-solvent attractions must be replaced by comparable solute-solvent ones; a hydroxyl group wins that contest for short chains but loses as the hydrocarbon fraction dominates the structure.
medium.analogy: A single anchor holds a dinghy in a storm, but the same anchor cannot hold a ferry - the polar group is the anchor, the growing chain is the ferry.
medium.examPointer: For 'why is hexanol insoluble' answers, blame the dominant non-polar chain diluting the one hydrogen-bonding site, not any failure of the OH group itself.

check.stem: What does 'like dissolves like' pair together?

options.text: Solutes and solvents with matching intermolecular force types
options.explanation: Matching forces let new solute-solvent attractions replace the old ones.
The principle spans all phase combinations.
Ionic solutes need polar, ion-surrounding solvents.
That is exactly the mismatch the principle rejects.

check.stem: Why does ethanol mix with water in all proportions?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds form between ethanol's O-H hydrogen and water's oxygens
options.explanation: The shared force type makes the pair interchangeable.
The hydrocarbon part is the insoluble end, not the mixer.
No ionisation occurs on mixing.
Both carry polar O-H groups.

check.stem: Why does hexanol dissolve poorly in water compared with ethanol?

options.text: Its long non-polar chain dilutes the one hydrogen-bonding site
options.explanation: The polar fraction shrinks as the chain grows.

options.text: Its OH group stops hydrogen bonding
options.explanation: The hydroxyl still works; the chain outvotes it.
Ethanol proves the opposite.
It remains a covalent molecular liquid.

check.stem: Why do giant covalent substances resist dissolving in every solvent?

options.text: Overcoming their covalent lattice bonds costs more energy than any solvent supplies
options.explanation: The network's bond energy prices it out of solution.

options.text: They are too light to sink into a solvent
options.explanation: Mass is irrelevant to solubility here.
No universal repulsion exists.

options.text: They hydrogen bond to themselves too strongly
options.explanation: Giant covalent networks have no molecular hydrogen bonding.

check.stem: A polar covalent solute lands in a non-polar solvent. What happens?

options.text: Its dipole-dipole attractions cannot interact well with the solvent, so it barely dissolves
options.explanation: The mismatch strands the solute.
That is the like-likes outcome, not this one.
Ionisation requires chemical reaction, not mixing.

options.text: It becomes non-polar to fit in
options.explanation: Molecules do not restructure to suit solvents.

check.stem: State the general principle governing solvent choice.
check.modelAnswer: Like dissolves like: non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents and polar substances dissolve in polar solvents, through matching force types.

check.stem: Quote the alcohol pair that demonstrates the chain-length effect on solubility.
check.modelAnswer: Ethanol, C2H5OH, is readily soluble in water while hexanol, C6H13OH, is not.

check.stem: Explain why solubility of covalent molecules can decrease as they become larger.
check.modelAnswer: The polar part of the molecule is a fixed fraction of its surface; as the molecule grows, that fraction shrinks relative to the non-polar bulk, so solvent contacts the polar site less often and dissolution pays worse.

check.stem: A series of alcohols adds CH2 per step, each step swelling the non-polar fraction by about 14 mass units against a fixed 17-unit OH group. Estimate the non-polar share for hexanol, C6H13OH, to the nearest whole percent.
check.modelAnswer: The chain carries 85 of 102 mass units, about 83 percent, leaving the tiny polar share that strands hexanol from water.

lessons.title: Haloalkanes in water and ions in polar solvents
lessons.opening: Two boundary cases complete the solvent map. This lesson shows why a polar C-X bond does not buy haloalkanes a seat in water, then follows water molecules as they pry an ionic lattice apart and surround each ion.
keyPoints: Haloalkanes are only partially soluble in water despite their polar C-X bond.
They cannot hydrogen bond because nothing in the molecule joins hydrogen to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen.
Water dissolves many ionic compounds by disrupting the lattice and surrounding the ions.
The positive cation is surrounded by delta-negative ends and the anion by delta-positive ends.
Higher ionic charge generally means lower solubility, with notable exceptions.

low.restatement: Polarity without a donor hydrogen leaves haloalkanes unable to join water's hydrogen-bond network; ions, by contrast, are welcomed because water wraps each one in the right end of its dipole.
low.analogy: A magnet (the polar bond) still cannot clip onto Velcro (the hydrogen-bond network); ions, however, walk straight into matching sockets at both poles of the water molecule.
low.examPointer: Say 'cannot form hydrogen bonds' as the haloalkane reason - writing 'they are non-polar' is chemically wrong and loses the mark.

medium.restatement: Dissolution of an ionic solid trades lattice electrostatics for hydration attractions; water's delta-positive hydrogens face the anion and its delta-negative oxygen faces the cation, and the balance tips worse as ionic charge grows.
medium.analogy: Lattice dissolution is a tug of war: the lattice rope (electrostatics) against two water ropes (hydration), and doubling the ionic charge thickens the lattice rope faster than water thickens theirs.
medium.examPointer: Compare the NaCl and CaCl2 solubility figures when asked for evidence - 356.9 g against 74.4 g per dm3 shows the charge penalty.

check.stem: Why are haloalkanes only partially soluble in water?

options.text: They cannot form hydrogen bonds with water
options.explanation: No bond in a haloalkane joins hydrogen to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen.
The C-X bond is polar; the hydrogen-bond capacity is what fails.
Alcohols dissolve readily.
The C-X bond is polar covalent, not ionic.

check.stem: Which feature would make a haloalkane more water-soluble?

options.text: Adding a hydroxyl group to the molecule
options.explanation: An O-H bond restores hydrogen-bond capacity, as in halogenated alcohols.

options.text: Replacing chlorine with a heavier halogen
options.explanation: Heavier halogens swell the non-polar fraction.
Longer chains worsen water solubility.
Polarity helps, not hurts.

check.stem: Which ends of water molecules surround a dissolved cation?

options.explanation: The negative pole faces the positive ion.
Like charges repel; that orientation cannot hold.
Ions contact lone-pair or dipole regions, not bond axes.
Hydration is oriented, not random.

check.stem: Why is calcium chloride less soluble in water than sodium chloride?

options.text: The 2+ cation's lattice attractions are stronger, and higher charge generally lowers solubility
options.explanation: Doubly charged ions hold the lattice harder.
It is an ionic compound.

options.text: Chloride ions are bigger in that salt
options.explanation: The anion is identical in both.
NaCl has no hydrogen at all.

check.stem: What two factors does the solubility of an ionic compound depend on?

options.text: Breaking down the ionic lattice and the surrounding of ions by polar molecules
options.explanation: Both costs and payoffs enter the balance.

options.text: Melting point and boiling point of the solute
options.explanation: Those are bulk properties, not the dissolution mechanism.

options.text: The colour and odour of the ions
options.explanation: Neither affects solubility.
The mechanism factors are lattice disruption and hydration.

check.stem: State what water does to an ionic lattice when a compound dissolves.
check.modelAnswer: Water disrupts the ionic lattice and surrounds each ion, with delta-positive hydrogens facing the anion and delta-negative oxygens facing the cation.

check.stem: Quote the solubility figures for sodium chloride and calcium chloride in one dm3 of water.
check.modelAnswer: About 356.9 g of sodium chloride dissolves per dm3 of water; calcium chloride manages only 74.4 g in that same volume.

check.stem: Explain why polarity alone does not make a compound water-soluble.
check.modelAnswer: Water's network is built of hydrogen bonds, so a compound joins it only by forming hydrogen bonds itself; a polar bond without a donor hydrogen, as in haloalkanes, offers nothing to that network and solubility stays partial.

check.stem: Sodium chloride dissolves 356.9 g per dm3 while calcium chloride manages 74.4 g. How many times more soluble, to one decimal place, is the sodium salt by these figures?
check.modelAnswer: Dividing 356.9 by 74.4 gives about 4.8, the solubility ratio that the charge penalty buys.

glossary.definition: The solvent-choice rule that solutes dissolve when their intermolecular forces match the solvent's.
The surrounding of dissolved ions by oriented polar solvent molecules, delta-negative ends to cations and delta-positive ends to anions.
A halogen-bearing alkane whose polar C-X bond cannot hydrogen bond, leaving it only partly soluble in water.
